analysis.one_liner: Ends logging, road-building, and mining in remaining old-growth federal forests in three Pacific states.
analysis.headline: Despite 139 cosponsors, the bill sat in two House committees for over a year, held hearings but never got a markup or floor vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a National Ancient Forest Reserve System out of the remaining old-growth ('ancient') forests on federal land in Washington, Oregon, and California. Inside those reserves, it would ban commercial timber sales, road construction, tree cutting, and most mining. It also would have given interim protection to every other qualifying old-growth stand, requiring the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management to cut their annual timber sales by the amount of timber removed from protection. The bill never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public: the bill's findings point to clean water supplies for downstream communities, habitat for salmon, steelhead, and the spotted owl, recreation, scientific and medical research value, and climate benefits from keeping ancient forests standing. Timber workers would have faced losses, addressed honestly under drawbacks.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a National Ancient Forest Reserve System and permanently bans road building, timber sales, and tree cutting within its units, while withdrawing those lands from mining, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing.

Extends interim protection to all federal forest land in Washington, Oregon, and California that qualifies as ancient or associated forest but is not formally designated, managed under the same no-logging rules until Congress acts otherwise.
Requires the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management to reduce annual timber sale offerings by the volume of commercially harvestable timber that had been available on protected land.
Directs the Council on Environmental Quality to convene a scientific panel to determine the biological and physical requirements for the survival of ancient forest ecosystems and report to Congress.

The bill's findings state that less than 2 percent of the nation's forested area remains ancient forest and that at the current rate, nearly all ecologically significant ancient forests would be destroyed within a decade.

analysis.who_pays: The timber industry, which would lose access to old-growth timber on federal lands; mills and logging-dependent communities in the Pacific Northwest, which would face reduced timber supply; and federal agencies, which must cut their sale programs accordingly.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself requires agencies to reduce annual timber sale offerings by an amount equal to the commercially harvestable timber removed from protection, cutting the raw material supply for mills and logging jobs in Washington, Oregon, and California.
The bill's own findings acknowledge that timber cutting rates in the Northwest would have to be reduced substantially, a cost its sponsor was asking the timber economy to bear.

It bars fire suppression inside reserve units except to protect human life or property, and bars suppression of native insects, plants, and diseases, a design choice that accepts natural fire and pest disturbance within the reserves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's environmental gains — permanent protection for what it describes as the last remnants of a nearly-liquidated ancient forest resource — were large and permanent, and it explicitly directed the agencies to reduce sale volumes by the protected amount rather than pretend the timber was still available. The cost fell on a specific region's timber industry and workers rather than on the public treasury, and the bill offered no transition assistance for displaced mill or logging workers, which is its most serious design gap for the people it most affected.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two committees and their subcommittees, held several hearings, but was never reported out, and the 102nd Congress ended with no House vote.

narrative.text: Introduced on February 6, 1991, the bill was referred jointly to the House Committee on Agriculture and the House Committee on Interior and Insular Affairs.
It was sent to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Forests, Family Farms, and Energy and the Interior Subcommittee on National Parks and Public Lands, which held hearings in April and May 1991.
No committee ever reported the bill, and no floor vote occurred. Its final recorded action, on May 7, 1992, was a cross-reference to H.R. 4899.
The bill drew 139 cosponsors — 119 Democrats, 19 Republicans, and 1 Independent — but that support never converted into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The timber industry and Pacific Northwest logging communities, which kept cutting old-growth federal timber under the pre-existing rules because the bill never moved.

for.name: Jim Jontz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ancient Forest Protection Act of 1991 and recruited a large bipartisan cosponsor list.

for.name: House Subcommittee on Forests, Family Farms, and Energy
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in April and May 1991, but never marked it up.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it died there more than a year after referral.

against.name: House Natural Resources (then Interior and Insular Affairs) Committee
against.what_they_did: Held subcommittee hearings but never reported the bill.

against.name: Timber industry
against.role: Pacific Northwest timber and wood products industry
against.what_they_did: The old-growth timber battles of this era drew intense industry lobbying against logging restrictions on federal land; no such activity appears in this bill's record.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but skewed Democratic: 119 of 267 House Democrats and 19 of 167 House Republicans cosponsored, and no vote ever occurred that would have split the chamber.

industries.note: The bill would have ended commercial harvest of old-growth federal timber and forced agencies to cut annual sale offerings by the protected volume, removing the industry's cheapest and largest raw material supply. Its gain in the actual outcome (the bill's death) came at the cost of the remaining ancient forests the public owns.

industries.industry: Pacific Northwest logging communities and mill towns
industries.note: Restricting old-growth harvest would have cost logging and milling jobs in the short term, while the bill's findings argue the forests' water, fisheries, and recreation values support broader economic stability and diversification in the region.
The bill cites the forests' outstanding recreational value for a growing population; protecting them intact preserves that benefit for the public.
